title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM‑Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced a single shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the same candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We (1) document the preregistered design, (2) present a compact formal scoring rule mapping archived validator/scorer outputs to the binary pass/fail labels used in the confirmatory test (with a concrete pass example from archived artifacts and a description of what a failing artifact would contain), (3) add a nearest-work comparison matrix contrasting this shared-generation paired design with the closest prior studies, and (4) provide artifact-grounded diagnostics, reproducibility guidance, and limitations.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) promise to translate operator intent into concrete network configuration commands, potentially improving NetOps productivity. However, syntactically plausible commands can violate workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without an enforced shutdown or performing hazardous uplink switchover), causing semantic failures only visible in closed-loop execution. Prior work therefore recommends integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment. Evaluating guarded pipelines requires executable tests that detect semantic and stateful failures beyond token- or syntax-level correctness.

We executed a preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that isolates the marginal effect of an executable validator and a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. The central confirmatory research question was: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair effects we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: each task produced one generator output that was scored both as baseline (LLM-only synthetic-apply) and as guarded (validator±repair). This design removes generator-induced variability across paired episodes and directly measures validator/repair influence on identical candidates.

Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120) that holds the generator fixed and measures the incremental effect of an executable validator plus bounded repair; (2) a compact formal definition of the binary pass/fail scoring rule used in the confirmatory McNemar test with an archival pass example and an explicit description of the archived fields that would indicate a fail; (3) a nearest-work comparison matrix that situates this shared-generation paired design relative to the closest executable-benchmark and agentic-NetOps studies; and (4) artifact-grounded execution accounting, diagnostics, and reproducibility guidance.
sections.related_work:
Two complementary research strands frame this study. (A) Executable, closed-loop benchmarks and verification tools demonstrate that text-level correctness does not guarantee safe enactment: closed-loop emulation exposes sequencing and stateful errors—make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, and required-ordered operations—that token- or syntax-only checks miss (see NetConfArena [https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23179], Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair [https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22513]). (B) Tool-augmented LLM agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canaries, translation-to-formal-model, generate→validate→repair) are widely proposed as operational safety measures (see MeshAgent/related agentic prototypes [https://doi.org/10.1145/3771567], Aether digital-twin work [https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18233], and architecture surveys [https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12729]). These studies generally test generator and verifier in coupled ways; systematic isolation of a verifier’s marginal effect under identical generator outputs is rare.

Nearest-work comparison matrix (compact):
- Protogeros et al. Benchmarking LLM-Driven Repair (arXiv:2604.22513): executable closed-loop benchmark; generator-focused evaluation across models; per-condition generation (not shared); emphasizes repair incidence across generators. Difference: this study uses a shared-generation paired design to isolate validator effects and uses a single-hosted model (gpt-5-mini).
- NetConfArena (arXiv:2608.23179): high-fidelity executable tasks; multiple generator/agent evaluations; focuses on closed-loop agent behavior. Difference: NetConfArena emphasizes model/agent variability; our paired design holds generator fixed to measure validator/repair marginality.
- MeshAgent (10.1145/3771567) and related agentic prototypes: end-to-end agent architectures with guardrails. Difference: these evaluate end-to-end agent improvements often with per-condition generation; we provide a complementary validator-focused lens and preregistered paired hypothesis test.
- Aether (arXiv:2604.18233) / Lightyear (10.1145/3603269.3604842): digital-twin and modular verification frameworks. Difference: these works emphasize tooling and verification scalability; our experiment addresses the marginal statistical effect of an executable validator plus bounded repair on identical generator outputs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) before execution. The preregistration specified a paired-binary confirmatory design with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks partitioned deterministically into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine) with 40 tasks each. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the prespecified test was the exact two-sided McNemar. A bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was included for the paired-difference estimate. The preregistration also defined exclusion/contamination rules, a repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), deterministic reset controls, and sensitivity analyses.

Task generation and structured payload. Tasks were produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, a natural-language intent, required_sequence (canonical ordered operations), and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level). The explicit required_sequence allows the emulator validator to check sequencing and workflow policies as structured constraints rather than relying on heuristic text matching.

Shared-generation paired design. For each task we performed a single shared initial candidate generation using the declared model (gpt-5-mini). The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 120 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}. This isolates the marginal effect of the validator/repair subsystem by removing generator variance across paired episodes. The trade-off is that if the generator systematically produces valid candidates, repair is unused—an anticipated risk discussed in the preregistration.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0), an executable emulator/validator that applies task-encoded workflow policies (for example: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break) and emits structured validator_trace fields: validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. The preregistered repair policy invoked at most one repair iteration when validator.violation_count>0; repair prompts and provider traces would be archived when generated. In this run validator.violation_count = 0 for all guarded episodes and no repair artifacts were generated.

Compact provenance pointer (moved from verbose manifest text). Primary archived artifacts required to reproduce reported accounting are available in the execution and analysis bundle: execution/raw_results.jsonl (raw episode records), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (task payloads and difficulty metadata), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (paired counts), analysis/condition_summary.csv (per-condition counts), analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json (provider-call audits and accounting), and execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini). These files and their recorded checksums are listed in the archived execution manifest; long file inventories and full hash manifests have been relocated to the supplementary execution bundle referenced by the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution summary and primary outcome. The run completed without technical exclusions: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Condition-level summaries record baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0, guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes.

Per-topology outcomes (counts). The deterministic task partition produced 40 tasks per topology class. Per-topology results are: Edge (40): baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Core (40): baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Leaf–spine (40): baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40. These counts are recorded in analysis/condition_summary.csv and the representative scoring artifacts (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json).

Formal binary scoring rule (compact, artifact-referent). The confirmatory binary label y_task,condition ∈ {pass, fail} used in McNemar was derived deterministically from archived scorer/validator outputs as follows (applied in order):
1) If scorer.scoring_status != "COMPLETED" or scorer.scorer_id != "deterministic_netops_validator_v5", then label = fail (technical/unscorable treated as exclusion per preregistration).  
2) Else, if scorer.score == 1 and validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true and validator_trace.validation_after.violation_count == 0, then label = pass.  
3) Else label = fail.  
This exact mapping was applied to each archived episode record when producing analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv. Concrete archived pass example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json shows scoring_status = "COMPLETED", score = 1, validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, and violation_count = 0 → label = pass. No archived episode contains violation_count > 0; therefore the dataset contains no concrete archived fail example. A failing archived record (had one occurred) would have contained either score != 1 or validator_trace.validation_after.valid = false and/or validator_trace.validation_after.violation_count > 0 and thus would be labeled fail under the rule above.

Repair activity and secondary endpoints. Because validator.violation_count = 0 for every guarded episode, repair_applied = false across the run and no repair_provider_trace artifacts exist. Preregistered secondary endpoints quantifying repair incidence and repair-call counts are therefore vacuous in this run; their vacuity is an empirical outcome recorded in validator traces and the execution manifest.

Contamination, missingness, and reconciliation. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 with zero technical/instrumentation exclusions. The deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms provider-audit counts and pair accounting are internally consistent (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cross-condition cache reuse = false).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The shared-generation paired design was chosen to answer a narrowly scoped mechanistic question—can a validator/repair subsystem improve outcomes for identical generator outputs? In this archived task bank and under the declared generator/prompt configuration the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator in all 120 pairs; consequently the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair behavior and could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline. The observed exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical expressions of this ceiling.

Design trade-offs and recommendations. The shared-generation protocol increases internal validity for isolating validator effects but may under-exercise repair when the generator is well-calibrated for the chosen task bank. From archived task_manifest difficulty metadata (fields: dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level) and the recorded absence of repairs, we recommend preregistered design adjustments for future confirmatory runs intended to measure repair utility: (a) independent per-condition generation (allow separate generator draws by condition) to expose generator variance; (b) controlled prompt perturbations on prespecified subsets to increase generator error incidence; (c) stratified sampling focused on tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count; (d) exploratory arms with expanded repair budgets and multiple repair iterations.

Operational implications and auditability. Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces (checked rules, touched fields, and why repair was not applied) supports operator auditability and post-hoc analysis. The archived artifacts demonstrate end-to-end instrumented accounting (provider-call audits, scoring traces, deterministic reconciliation) that can be repurposed for operator-facing explanations and third-party audits. The experiment underlines that claims about repair benefits require careful experimental framing: if generators rarely produce invalid candidates under a given prompt, the guard will be idle by design.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by the validator’s policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads; while required_sequence enforces canonical workflows, the validator does not emulate every vendor-specific behavior or partial-observability telemetry. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power calculation assumed baseline failure ≈0.40 and targeted absolute reduction 0.15; observed baseline = 0.00 violates those assumptions and makes the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness with a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, yielding n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling for this curated synthetic task bank and illustrates that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we show how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts permit follow-up studies that relax the shared-generation constraint, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
